heading: Your next steps
intro: Suplex checks zoning only. These are the steps that usually come next after a screening like this.

groups.alternatives: If the free designs don't fit

footer: Every project is different, and Suplex can't tell you what your project will need. Screening only, not a permit or legal advice. Steps and contacts come from City of Toronto pages checked on {checked_on}; confirm with the City before you rely on them.

survey.title: Get a current survey of your lot
survey.text: The City's pre-approved plans need a survey or site plan with property lines referenced to a current survey, and a zoning review asks for a current land survey prepared by a licensed Ontario Land Surveyor. Suplex measures from City lot lines, which are not survey-accurate.

sources.quote: Property lines, lot area, right-of-way or easements (referenced to a current survey)
Survey or site plan showing property lines, lot area, right-of-way or easements (based on a current land survey prepared by a licensed Ontario Land Surveyor).

zoning_check.title: Check the zoning with the City
zoning_check.text: Toronto Building staff can answer zoning questions about this specific property: 416-397-5330, Monday to Friday, 8:30 a.m. to 4:30 p.m. For a written answer before you apply, a Zoning Applicable Law Certificate reviews your drawings (up to three reviews); if you apply for the building permit with the certificate, its fee is credited against the building permit fees. A Property Information Report ($214.79) lists the building permits issued for an address, the status of their inspections and any outstanding orders.

sources.quote: If you have zoning questions for a specific property, please contact Toronto Building Staff at 416-397-5330 between 8:30 a.m. to 4:30 p.m., Monday to Friday or in person at a Toronto Building Customer Service counter.
An application for a Zoning Applicable Law Certificate includes a maximum of three reviews.

the fee paid for the Zoning Applicable Law Certificate will be credited to the building permit application such that the building permit fees will be reduced by the amount of the Zoning Applicable Law Certificate fee.
provides information for a specific municipal address regarding issued building permits on file

site_exception.title: Look up site-specific exception x{number}
site_exception.text: Your zone label carries site-specific exception x{number}. A Chapter 900 exception may set limits that still apply to a multiplex, such as a maximum floor space index or lot coverage. Suplex does not read exceptions. Look it up on the City's Interactive Zoning By-law Map or ask zoning staff on 416-397-5330.
site_exception.text_without_number: Your zone label carries a site-specific exception. A Chapter 900 exception may set limits that still apply to a multiplex, such as a maximum floor space index or lot coverage. Suplex does not read exceptions. Look it up on the City's Interactive Zoning By-law Map or ask zoning staff on 416-397-5330.

sources.quote: If there is a Chapter 900 exception which applies to the property, indicated by an (x) followed by a number in the zone label, any maximum floor space index specified in this exception may still apply.

If your property is subject to lot coverage as indicated by the Lot Coverage Overlay, the base residential standards in Chapter 10, or a Chapter 900 exception, this regulation still applies to multiplexes.

heritage.title: Talk to Heritage Planning
heritage.text: This property is on the City's Heritage Register or in a Heritage Conservation District. In a district, new construction, exterior alterations and additions need a heritage permit. On an individually designated property, altering or demolishing a building needs heritage permission, and some decisions go to City Council. A listed property has no protection under the Ontario Heritage Act, except that its owner must give City Council at least 60 days' notice before demolishing. Heritage Planning can advise before you design.

sources.quote: New construction, exterior alterations, and additions to properties within an HCD will require a heritage permit and will need to meet the policies of the relevant HCD Plan, as well as other City requirements.
Permission is required for work that involves altering, demolishing/removing or erecting a building or structure on properties that are designated under Part IV of the Ontario Heritage Act.
For applications that do not have delegated approval authority Heritage Planning will have to seek a decision from City Council.

Non-designated listed properties do not have any protection under the Ontario Heritage Act, except insofar as an owner must give the council at least 60 days' notice of their intention to demolish or remove a structure on the property.

ravine.title: Check ravine and natural feature protection
ravine.text: Part of this lot is in a ravine or natural feature protection area. The City requires a ravine permit before anyone harms or removes a tree there of any size, changes the natural land topography (digging, or adding soil on slopes), places fill, or builds or replaces structures or retaining walls.
ravine.who: Tree and Ravine Protection, City of Toronto

links.label: When to apply for a tree or ravine permit

sources.quote: Harming or removing any trees, regardless of size
Changing the natural land topography, by excavation or adding soil or other materials on slopes
Constructing new or replacing old structures or retaining walls

trca.title: Ask the conservation authority
trca.text: If your lot is in the Toronto and Region Conservation Authority's regulated area, building or replacing a home usually needs a TRCA permit under Ontario Regulation 41/24, and the City cannot issue a building permit until TRCA has issued a permit or clearance. TRCA encourages talking to one of its planners before you apply.

sources.quote: Building a new home (or a replacement home) is considered DEVELOPMENT ACTIVITY under the Conservation Authorities Act and Ontario Regulation 41/24.
your municipality cannot legally issue a building permit until a TRCA permit or clearance has been obtained.
Toronto and Region Conservation Authority (TRCA) encourages clients to discuss their proposals with a TRCA Planner prior to submitting a permit application.

trees.title: Check the trees
trees.text: Trees 30 cm or more in diameter on your lot, and City street trees of any size, need a tree permit before any work that could injure or remove them. Having a building permit does not remove that need. The building permit application also includes a Tree Declaration Form.

links.label: When to apply for a tree or ravine permit

sources.quote: Any activity that can cause a tree of 30 centimetres or more in diameter, to be injured or removed, on private property, is prohibited unless authorized with a permit under the Tree Protection By-law.
Any activity that can cause a street tree of any size to be harmed or removed is prohibited unless authorized with a permit under the Tree Protection By-law.
If your as-of-right development impacts a protected tree, you are still required to apply for a permit to remove or injure it.
Required for all projects where there is a potential for damage to private or City trees.

designer.title: Work with a design professional
designer.text: A qualified design professional finishes the site-specific parts: the site plan, the lot grading plan, the zoning and code matrices on sheets A010 and A011, and signed and sealed architectural, structural and mechanical letters. Changing the plan itself, even the heating or plumbing, means it is no longer pre-approved.

sources.quote: While the plans have been pre-approved, a qualified design professional is still required to review, assume responsibility for, and finalize all site-specific aspects of the design in accordance with the Building Code and the Building Code Act.

If any modifications are made to the pre-approved plan selected, including HVAC or plumbing modifications, the plan will no longer be considered pre-approved, and this process for applying for a building permit will NOT apply.

permit.title: Apply for the building permit
permit.text: Apply online through Toronto Building and enter the pre-approved plan number on the Application to Construct or Demolish; you do not resubmit the City's drawings. The application also includes forms such as the Infill Public Notice Declaration Form and the Municipal Road Damage Form.

sources.quote: When applying for a building permit, enter the pre-approved plan number on the Application to Construct or Demolish form. You do not need to submit the pre-approved drawing.

Required Forms, "Infill Public Notice Declaration Form": "This is a declaration form to be submitted to Toronto Building in order for the Owner or authorised agent of the owner to request an electronic copy of the Residential Infill Public Notice from Toronto Building"

Required Forms, "Municipal Road Damage Form": "Applicant/owner is required to pay a damage deposit as a protection guarantee against damage to the curb, sidewalk, road, public laneway, boulevard and other services as well as tracking mud on City streets, or failing to clear snow and ice from sidewalks while construction is in progress."

demolition.title: Add a demolition permit
demolition.text: Replacing the existing house also needs a demolition permit. When you apply online, you can add the demolition permit after you submit the building permit application, using the reference number and access code from your confirmation email.

sources.quote: When submitting your application online, you can also apply for related demolition, mechanical, plumbing, and drain permits after submitting your building permit application.

fees.title: Check development charges
fees.text: Under By-law 845-2025 (July 24, 2025), a multiplex of up to six units pays no development charges on its second, third and fourth units, and the fifth and sixth are reduced to $0. Parkland cash-in-lieu is waived for the second to sixth unit. These apply when the parcel has no more than six units (a garden or laneway suite on the City's development charges deferral program does not count toward that six; for parkland, a garden or laneway suite allows up to seven in total). Some City web pages still say four units; the by-law is the current rule.

sources.quote: (a) Shall not be imposed with respect to the second, third or fourth residential dwelling unit; and
(b) For the fifth or sixth residential dwelling unit, shall be reduced to zero dollars ($ 0.00);

provided that such exemption applies to developments of no more than six total residential dwelling units (or seven residential dwelling units where there is a Garden or Laneway Suite) on a single parcel of land

attached_options.title: Look at options for a semi or row house
attached_options.text: The City's free designs are for detached lots. On a semi or row-house lot you may still convert part of the existing house to up to four homes if the new homes fit entirely inside the building as it stood before May 15, 2023, or add a garden suite where the rules allow. A semi or a row house cannot be converted to a fiveplex or sixplex (By-law 654-2025, 600.60.40(3)(D)).

sources.quote: In the Residential Zone category, a portion of a semi-detached house located on one lot may be converted to contain up to four dwelling units
(A) the original building was constructed prior to May 15, 2023 and the additional dwelling units are contained entirely within the lawfully existing building

In the Residential Zone category, a portion of a townhouse located on one lot may be converted to contain up to four dwelling units and may continue to be considered as a townhouse despite the building type definitions in Chapter 800 provided:
(A) if the original building was constructed prior to May 15, 2023 and the additional dwelling units are contained entirely within the lawfully existing building
no portion of a semi-detached houseplex, a semi-detached house or a townhouse may be converted to a fiveplex or sixplex through the construction of additional dwelling units.

custom_or_variance.title: Look at other options
custom_or_variance.text: None of the City's four designs fits as checked. A design professional can prepare a custom design and apply through the regular building permit process. If that design goes beyond the zoning rules, you can apply to the Committee of Adjustment for a minor variance; approval is not assured.
custom_or_variance.who: A design professional; the Committee of Adjustment

sources.quote: You can apply to the City of Toronto Committee of Adjustment to request a minor variance to the Zoning By-law.
You may apply for a building permit through the regular application process.
